beats.trigger: ## From Personal to Team
beats.got: nothing new

beats.trigger: You can't really share an agent.
beats.got: Sharing an agent isn't one thing. It splits into context, skill, output or interface. The first sentence is at least a plain claim.

beats.trigger: **Bring one example from your own organisation where people got access to a tool and did not use it.**
beats.got: They want my own failure case, not theirs. I have three of those in the drawer, so this is the first thing that is actually about me.

beats.trigger: **Find** the absorption bottleneck and draft the technical plan and the people plan together
beats.got: nothing new. It is a learning-objectives list, and I have seen this slide in every programme.

beats.trigger: your `memory/` folder, one of your skills, the morning output, or a way to ask the agent a question in Slack
beats.got: They assume I already have a memory folder, skills and a morning output. I don't. I'm not sure I'm in the right room.

beats.trigger: Your agent, skill, output or interface is a candidate for hire: does it do the job better than what they currently use?
beats.got: Jobs-to-be-Done applied to colleagues. It is a known framework, and at least it is a reasonable question to ask.

beats.trigger: [You paste prompt "share-your-work-1" into Claude and it works on it.]
beats.got: I paste something and it works. I never see what the prompt says or what came back, so I can't judge it. I have to take it on faith.

beats.trigger: *"Share the whole agent"* is not on the list.
beats.got: There are four ways to share, and the obvious one, handing over the agent, is ruled out. That is a candid limit, and I like that.

beats.trigger: [Design the sharing plan](design-the-sharing-plan.md) finds what would stop that candidate from being absorbed
beats.got: nothing new. It is a link to the next exercise.

beats.trigger: Find the obstacle that decides whether the teammate can absorb it, then draft both halves of the plan.
beats.got: nothing new. More plan files.

beats.trigger: A good bottleneck explains why several other obstacles stay hard.
beats.got: Look for the root cause, not the first symptom. That is root-cause analysis with a new name, but it is sensible.

beats.trigger: A polished technical file beside a people file full of unnamed roles is the finding, not a finished rollout.
beats.got: The plan's own gaps count as the result, and the exercise says so. Every programme I've sat through had the polished half and the empty half.

beats.trigger: checks the assumptions underneath these plans, imagines the failure, and writes the first real-world contact
beats.got: nothing new. Another link.

beats.trigger: The technical and people plans are hypotheses.
beats.got: The plans are guesses until tested. Fine, and it is the first thing that sounds like how I'd work.

beats.trigger: what would have to be true for this teammate, doing this job, to fire their current hire and use my candidate?
beats.got: Don't ask how to get them to adopt it. Ask what would have to be true for them to switch. That is a useful reframe, even without the AI part.

beats.trigger: Six months from now, the teammate went back to the incumbent.
beats.got: A pre-mortem ending in one named person and one question. It is small and doable without any technology.

beats.trigger: A candidate picked because it fits the infrastructure is shopping.
beats.got: Pick for the outcome, not for the platform. It is sound advice, and I could have written it without any of the exercises.

beats.trigger: ## Lecture: Access is not absorption
beats.got: nothing new. The title is the point, and I already agree with it from three licence rollouts.

beats.trigger: Access is a switch somebody flips, and it completes in a minute.
beats.got: The rollout dashboard counts access, but uptake happens in people's weeks. This matches what I've watched for twenty years.

beats.trigger: The proposal got neither a yes nor a no.
beats.got: A trainer who admits his own project died in a leadership non-decision. It is candid, and I've lived that exact meeting.

beats.trigger: Accountability is the part with a name on it, and a name does not travel inside a folder.
beats.got: You can copy the context, the boundary and the checks, but not who answers for it. The line is a bit neat, but the point is true.

beats.trigger: Pick the one your teammate's week can take in.
beats.got: Each sharing option demands different things from the receiver, so choose by what their week allows.

beats.trigger: Your candidate is not competing with nothing. It is competing with that.
beats.got: The thing I'm replacing is a spreadsheet or a gut call that has worked for years, and it's the real competitor. That's why people ignore the new tool.

beats.trigger: Have the conversation before you build anything more.
beats.got: Talk to one person before building more. Small and cheap, which I can do.

beats.trigger: [You paste prompt "a101-m7-debrief-sharing-artifact" into Claude and it works on it.]
beats.got: nothing new. Another prompt I never see, producing an artifact I can't inspect.

beats.trigger: Access is a switch someone flips. Absorption happens in other people's weeks.
beats.got: A recap. The last line is the only one I'd keep.

beats.trigger: Their answer is the evidence. The plan is still the hypothesis.
beats.got: Bring what the person actually said, not the plan. It is honest, and it makes me test the claim myself.

beats.trigger: ## Next
beats.got: nothing new

take_homes: Rollouts report access as if it were uptake. Whoever flips the switch is not the person whose week has to change.
The thing to ask is not how to get people to adopt it but what would have to be true for them to drop what they use now. The answer is probably small and specific.
Talk to one named person about how they do the job today before building anything more.

monday.move: Pick the last tool rollout nobody used, and ask one team lead how they do that job today. I won't touch any agent stuff.
monday.who: One team lead from the last programme's steering group
monday.when: Tuesday or Wednesday, in a 15-minute chat
monday.stop_condition: They describe a current way of working that already works well enough and they see no reason to switch. Then I stop.
monday.blocker: The calendar full of steering groups, and no hands-on agent experience. I'd have no idea what to share.

misconception.why: The module mostly agrees with my scepticism about rollouts and doesn't oversell, which helps. But I never saw a real agent do something that wasn't possible two years ago. The prompts ran off-screen, so 'this will blow over' is only dented, not changed.

one_line: The honest bit about adoption is good, and the story of the decision that never came is the best part. But I never saw the agent actually do anything, so I can't tell whether it's different from the last three.
